HowItWorks: A recruiter says you are hired and sends a check for supplies or a signing bonus. They tell you to deposit it and forward the extra money before the bank confirms the check is real.
RedFlags: The check shows up before a real interview, and they rush you to wire or send money the same day.
ExampleMessage: Congrats, you're hired! Deposit this $3,200 check today and send $2,400 to our equipment vendor so we can ship your laptop.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not deposit the check. Contact your bank if money was sent, and report the recruiter on JobLens.

HowItWorks: The sender says the company will pay you back for a laptop or home-office kit, but you must buy it from their vendor first.
RedFlags: They will not let you use a normal store, and the vendor only takes gift cards, wires, or payment apps.
ExampleMessage: Order your work laptop from our approved vendor today. We will reimburse the full cost on your first paycheck.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not pay the vendor. Verify the job on the company's official careers page, then report the message on JobLens.

HowItWorks: After a short chat, the recruiter says you must pay a training, background-check, or onboarding fee before you can start.
RedFlags: A real employer does not make students pay to get hired, especially with a gift card or instant payment.
ExampleMessage: Your offer is ready, but pay a $150 onboarding fee by gift card today so we can release your start date.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not send any payment. Contact the USF Career Services office and report the request on JobLens.

HowItWorks: Someone posing as a recruiter runs the whole interview in Telegram, WhatsApp, or Signal and never uses a company video call.
RedFlags: They avoid an official email or campus interview and push you onto a private chat app.
ExampleMessage: I'm a recruiter at Deloitte. Join me on Telegram tonight for your interview, and please do not email our main office.
WhatToDo: Stop replying in the chat app. Verify the role on the official careers page and report the account on JobLens.

HowItWorks: The email looks like it came from a famous company, but the domain is slightly wrong, with a swapped letter or an extra word.
RedFlags: The address is not the company's real domain, and the message pushes you to act before you look closely.
ExampleMessage: This is Amazon Talent. Confirm your internship today by replying to hr@amaz0n-careers.net with your phone number.
WhatToDo: Stop replying. Compare the domain with the official careers page, then report the email on JobLens.

ScamName: Recruiter using a personal email (gmail / outlook)
HowItWorks: A person says they hire for a well-known employer, but they write from Gmail, Outlook, or another free inbox.
RedFlags: The company is famous, yet the sender cannot use a company email address.
ExampleMessage: Hi, I hire interns for Microsoft. Email me at recruiter.mike@gmail.com and I will send your offer.
WhatToDo: Stop replying until you can verify the person. Check the official careers page or contact the USF Career Services office, then report the message on JobLens.

HowItWorks: The posting offers easy pay for receiving packages at home and mailing them to another address.
RedFlags: They want your home address right away, and the packages come from strangers rather than the company.
ExampleMessage: Work from your dorm as a logistics assistant. Packages arrive this week; relabel them and ship them out for $400 a week.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not accept any packages. Report the offer on JobLens and contact the USF Career Services office.

HowItWorks: The ad promises high pay for simple typing or data entry, with almost no experience and no real interview.
RedFlags: The pay is far above a normal student job, and the next step is often a fee for software or a starter kit.
ExampleMessage: Earn $35 an hour entering data from home. No experience needed. Reply now and we will send the signup form.
WhatToDo: Stop replying if they ask for money or personal documents. Verify any real employer on the official careers page and report the ad on JobLens.

ScamName: SSN or bank details requested before an offer
HowItWorks: The recruiter asks for your Social Security number, a photo of your ID, or your bank login before a verified employer has given you a written offer.
RedFlags: They call it a background check or payroll setup, but you have not met anyone from the company.
ExampleMessage: To finish your background check, send a photo of your ID and your Social Security number in this chat.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not send those details. Contact the USF Career Services office and report the request on JobLens.

HowItWorks: A supposed staffing firm says it can place you at a famous company, but the agency itself is not a real hiring partner.
RedFlags: You cannot find the firm on the employer's site, and the recruiter will not name a real hiring manager.
ExampleMessage: Our agency is filling JPMorgan internships this week. Send your resume, address, and date of birth so we can submit you today.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not send personal records. Confirm the agency with the USF Career Services office or on the official careers page, then report it on JobLens.

HowItWorks: The job asks you to receive other people's money in your account and forward it, often under a title like payment processor.
RedFlags: Your only task is moving money, and they want your bank login or debit card.
ExampleMessage: You will be our payment processor. Customers deposit funds into your account, and you keep 10 percent when you wire the rest.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and never move money for them. Contact your bank if money was sent, and report the job on JobLens.

HowItWorks: The sender promises a job, visa, or sponsorship only after you pay a processing fee.
RedFlags: They pressure you to pay before any official offer, and the money goes to a person instead of a government office.
ExampleMessage: We can sponsor your work visa, but you must pay a $500 processing fee today to lock your slot.
WhatToDo: Stop replying and do not pay the fee. Contact the USF Career Services office and report the offer on JobLens.
